Good afternoon, members of council, staff, and the public.
I'm here to provide an overview of Corporate Services Report 2024-007, Methods to Fill a Vacancy for the Ward 10 Office.
The report before you provides Council with various methods and considerations on how best to fill the vacancy.
Following the resignation of the Ward 10 member, Council declared the Ward 10 seat vacant on December 14, 2023,
and now Council is required within 60 days to determine the method they want to fill the vacancy.
There are two options set out in legislation, either by appointment or by by-election,
and those methods are further defined in the following slides.
It is important to note that the Act does not specify requirements relating to the appointment of an individual to fill a council vacancy, other than requiring the appointed member to be eligible.
The options presented are based on best practice.
There are three different appointment processes possible.
1A is to appoint a candidate from the 2022 municipal election candidates for Ward 10, and typically this is done to the next person in line in terms of the highest number of votes received in 2022.
1B is the appointment of an eligible elector through an established formal selection process,
and that process is further outlined in the appendices to your report being the Council appointment procedure.
1C would be the appointment of an eligible elector without a formal selection process at Council's choice.
Each option is further defined.
option 1a the appointment of a candidate from the 2022 municipal election would require the
clerk to confirm that the candidate is qualified in consents to the office if both conditions are
met an appointment bylaw would be brought forward for consideration at a subsequent council meeting
this option results in the fastest filling of the vacancy by the end of january with no costs
Option 1B, an open call for applications would require Council approval of the procedures,
including the application form included in the appendices.
This would initiate a public process where notices circulated for a minimum of two weeks.
Members of the public could apply to fill the vacancy using the required forms.
Once the Clerk confirms the candidates are qualified, the applications would be placed on an agenda,
applicants permitted to address Council regarding their application and the community to be involved.
Members of Council could ask the candidates questions
and the successful candidate would be determined by the approved balloting process.
This option results in Council considering the applicants by the end of January
with the members selected and sworn into office by the end of February.
There are nominal costs with this option to post notices in the newspaper and on social media.
Option 1C, the direct appointment of a candidate without a formal process, would require the clerk to confirm that the candidate is qualified and consents to the office.
If both conditions are met, like in Option 1A, an appointment bylaw would be brought forward to consideration at a subsequent council meeting.
This option, like 1A, results in the fastest filling of the vacancy by the end of January with no costs.
The second option is to direct the city clerk to initiate a by-election to fill the vacancy.
To do this, Council is required to pass a by-election by-law within 60 days of the vacancy.
The proposed by-election by-law is attached to the report.
By-elections are administered under Section 65 of the Municipal Elections Act,
and the timing of nomination day and voting day are prescribed in the legislation.
The Act states that by-elections are held in the same manner as the original general election.
In 2022, paper ballots were used with a vote count tabulator.
The timeline that staff have proposed is an aggressive one
to ensure that Ward 10 residents have representation on council
within approximately four months from the vacancy being declared,
while providing an adequate campaign period and time for voters to vote.
Staff have proposed that nomination processes would commence this week
and close on February 23rd at 2 p.m., allowing 45 days for nomination filing.
Voting day would then occur 45 days later on Monday, April 8th,
with three advance voting days held the week prior on April 4th, 5th, and 6th.
Election results would be confirmed shortly thereafter,
and the candidate could be sworn into office at the end of April.
Staff have obtained quotations for the most financially significant components of a by-election,
including the voting equipment, voter notification cards, and Canada Post mailing costs.
These costs are based on running a ward by-election on the same parameters as the 2022 general election,
and total between $77,000 and approximately $100,000.
It is important to note that these costs do not include the salaries and wages
for an election project manager, which is typically hired to assist with project planning,
any costs related to hiring members of the public to work the municipal election,
or required advertisements and notices that the Act's dates must be placed in a newspaper.
If a by-election is selected, staff have recommended that due to resources and election activities,
the approved 2024 Council meeting schedule be amended for March and April.
So in summary, the next steps would be for Council to determine which option they would like to proceed with
to fill the vacancy for the Ward 10 Councillor.
The recommendation in the report requires an option to be inserted.
If option 1A or 1C is selected, an additional paragraph is recommended to direct the Clerk
to confirm the qualifications and consent of the candidate
and bring forward the appointment bylaw for adoption at the next council meeting.
If option 1B is selected, an additional paragraph is recommended
to approve the application procedures for implementation.
And lastly, if option 2 is selected, two additional paragraphs are recommended
to bring forward the required by-election bylaw
and to amend the 2024 council and committee meeting calendar.
Staff will proceed with planning for whatever option is selected this afternoon.

I have five minutes, so let's first look at our neighbours' approaches.
All in 2023, Cambridge City Council and two local school boards faced vacancies created by resignation or the passing of the incumbent.
The school boards both chose appointments over by-elections, weighing cost and democratic engagement.
The public board invited applications and trustees chose from amongst them in a process that was created transparently, but it included some very opaque aspects.
The Catholic board considered only those that had been candidates in the last general election and chose a runner-up from a different constituency than the one that was vacant.
Cambridge City Council faced a decision on how to fill the vacancy created by the passing of Ward 1 Councillor Donna Reed.
They chose a by-election, and in the end, the voters chose the person who had been runner-up in the 2022 election.
These cases highlight diverse approaches to a common challenge, underscoring that there's no one-size-fits-all solution.
Now let's pivot to the current predicament here at Kitchener City Council.
A by-election, while democratic, comes with hefty costs and typically low turnout.
A low turnout election could easily lead to questions about the winner's legitimacy.
Conversely, council appointments could be perceived as biased, akin to choosing your
favourite niece or nephew. It's tricky and might not sit well with everyone.
Additionally, in a process that considers runner-up candidates, of which I note I am
one, I'm concerned about the precedent. Should a bad actor realise that they can
replace an undesirable, to them at least, incumbent with a runner-up that is more palatable,
they might be emboldened to wage a campaign of harassment or bullying designed to lead
to that incumbent's resignation. Directly appointing a runner-up might inadvertently
promote a culture of hostility against elected officials potentially encouraging resignations
to pave the way for preferred candidates. While I haven't seen much indication of this
at the City Council, I've certainly seen a lot of vitriol directed towards certain members
of our local school boards, both online and in delegations. Our councillors, of course,
will know what arrives in their inbox much better than I do.

through appointment.

diverse randomly selected Kitchener residents would deliberate on a process and eventually
on the candidates.

to make an informed decision.
Kitchener City Council would commit to appointing the candidate recommended by this assembly.

that the new Councillor is chosen and empowered by collective wisdom rather than fiscal constraints
or political maneuvering.

of citizens' assemblies in action in a new and innovative application.
